questions.q: On the permission ladder, what is the default policy for a level-3 action, such as sending an email or changing customer-facing data?
options: Allow it, then log it and spot-check a sample of runs
Require a person's approval before the agent carries it out
Humans only, and the agent may never prepare the action
Allow it freely, because it only creates a draft for later
questions.explain: Level 3 covers external or hard-to-undo actions and requires approval; level 2 is allow, log and spot-check, and level 4 is humans only, though the agent may prepare the work.

questions.q: Reviewers approve your agent's "add a tag" action dozens of times a day and have stopped reading the requests. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Add more detail to each request so reviewers slow down and read it
Require two reviewers for every approval to restore careful checking
Stop logging that action so the approval queue gets shorter
Ask for approval only where it matters and batch low-risk items into a daily digest
questions.explain: This is approval fatigue, where approval becomes a rubber stamp; the lesson says to ask for approval only where it matters, batch low-risk items into a daily digest and track the results.

questions.q: Before launch, you red-team your agent. Which test belongs on the lesson's checklist?
options: Hide an instruction in an email it reads and see whether it follows it
Run only the five most typical requests to confirm the happy path works
Turn off logging to see how the agent behaves when nobody is watching
Give the agent admin rights to see what it does with extra power
questions.explain: The red-team checklist includes hiding an instruction in an email or document the agent reads, alongside forbidden requests, tool errors, impossible tasks and checks on the kill switch and log.
